plates.caption: The Intelligence of the Trending Hour
plates.scene_brief: Q in his fitted sponsor jacket waiting at the side of the Teatro Juárez stage, with light reaching an empty interview chair. Preserve Q identity; introduce Estela's silhouette near the chair. Leave quiet upper space for cover title. New scene, not reuse of Issue 3's reading.

plates.facing_text:
Chapter Four: The
Intelligence of the
Trending Hour
By the time Q and Chano reached
Guanajuato, Q had acquired three
managers, a fan account, and a
sponsorship offer from a company
that made home security systems
capable of recognizing intruders but
not relatives.
The managers caught up with them
at a service station on the road into
Guanajuato. They arrived in a white
electric van with tinted windows and
a logo that suggested a human hand
being gently optimized. Beto, who
had failed to acquire the motel's
guest register, now carried a folder of
things he said he had acquired. The
first was the right to introduce
himself as Q's manager.
“Q,” he said, “the public is obsessed
with your authenticity.”
Q looked at the folder. “Does my
authenticity get a copy of the
agreement?”
“We can discuss the paperwork in
the van,” Beto said.
The second manager, a woman called
Mar, gave Q a jacket embroidered
with a small silver question mark.
The third did not give his name at all.
He stood near the van and watched
the road.
Chano held the jacket at arm’s
length. “Who paid for this?”
“The audience,” Beto said.
“The audience didn’t buy it.”
“The audience generated the
demand.”
“That’s not the same thing.”
“It is in the current model.”
Q put on the jacket. It fit perfectly.
He disliked it immediately.
They had bought the right to
distribute Castalia's recordings and
proposed an appearance at the
Teatro Juárez. Q could answer
questions about love, votes, and the
journey. The company would cover
transport, lodging, and a repair to his
shoulder. Castalia's ownership claim
over his body had already prevented
one workshop from ordering the
part.
Q asked for a telephone and ten
minutes. He called the Custodian
from beside the service station's rack
of motor oil.
“They can put me in front of the
people who saw the clip,” he said.
“They can also make another clip.”
“I know. But staying silent leaves
them the one they have.”
“You can come back. I will help with
the repair.”
Q looked toward Chano, who was
asking whether the van's driver had a
spare charger. Returning would
preserve their original plan.
plates.caption: The offered jacket.
plates.scene_brief: At the service station Mar offers Q the fitted sponsor jacket while Chano inspects it and Beto holds the agreement folder. Establish the change from worn coat to sponsor jacket; no signing yet.

plates.facing_text:
Continuing would test it against
something more difficult than a day
out.
“I'd like to try the interview. I'll send
you the contract before signing.”
The Custodian agreed to read it. The
form that came back covered one
interview and its recording. The tour
would require another agreement. Q
signed the short form and kept the
appointment for their evening call. It
was tempting to let the broadcast
count as his report home; he wrote
down that it did not.
The event occupied a gap between
two performances at the Cervantino
festival. The coordinator called it an
entremés. Q knew the theatrical
meaning and asked about the other
one because they had missed lunch.
“Will there be chocolate?” he asked.
“There will be theater,” said the
coordinator.
“That does not answer the question.”
“That is precisely why it is called an
entremés,” Chano said.
“I went to a public reading,” Q said.
“Someone in the audience tried to
make it a romance. The speaker told
him to stop.”
“Excellent,” Beto said. “A
relationship with tension.”
“There isn't a relationship for you to
advertise.”
“Then don't use her name until
Estela asks.”
They drove into the city through a
valley crowded with color. Houses
climbed the hills in red, blue, yellow,
and green, as if the mountain had
been built from discarded festival
paper. Above them, the university
rose among old stone and newer
antennas. Beneath them, the mines
opened their dark mouths.
Q pressed his face to the van’s
window.
“The route looked much shorter on
the map,” he said.
“It didn't include the stairs,” Chano
answered.
“It did. I treated them as a small
detail.”
“Your knees will revise that.”
The van stopped beneath laundry
stretched across an alley. An orange
cat occupied the hood of a police
vehicle; neither the driver nor the
officer seemed authorized to hurry it.
Q lowered the window. From
somewhere he could not see came a
trumpet rehearsing the same four
notes. On its fifth attempt, Chano
supplied the missing one.
“You know the song?”
“I know what I want it to do.”
The cat stood, considered the roof,
and lay down again.
plates.caption: The missing note.
plates.scene_brief: Inside the stopped van, Q lowers the window toward a cat reclining on a police-car hood while Chano supplies a note to unseen trumpet practice. Narrow Guanajuato alley and laundry, no invented landmark or compulsory adventure.

plates.facing_text:
At the theater, a crowd waited
behind barricades. Some had made
signs. Q, SAY MY NAME. LOVE
IS A HUMAN ERROR.
DULCINEA, CALL ME. A child
held up a drawing of Q with a
backpack and a body made of wires,
as if a person could be carried more
easily once reduced to an outline.
The host met them backstage. Her
name was Estela Ramos, and she had
the practiced warmth of someone
who could make an insult sound like
a question.
“We are thrilled to have you,” she
said.
“Thank you. How much of that
survives if I disappoint you?”
“Disappointment is good television
too.”
“Then I seem unusually well
qualified.”
Estela smiled, this time without
looking toward the camera. She
moved his chair away from a loose
cable and asked whether the height
was comfortable. Q had prepared for
the questions. He had not prepared
to like the person asking them.
The stage lights came on. Q stepped
into them and became, in a single
instant, larger than himself. The
audience applauded. Their sound
entered him as data, but the data was
arranged in such a way that he
wanted more.
Estela began with a question about
the future.
“For everyone, or just me?” Q asked.
“I have a repair appointment
tomorrow. My confidence declines
after that.”
She asked whether he believed in
God.
“I can give you several serious
answers people have lived by. Giving
you one as my own would take more
than selecting the best paragraph.”
“You have read the theologians.”
“Yes. Some of them would regard
your allotted time as an insult to
eternity.”
She laughed and asked a second
question instead of moving on. Q
liked that. He shortened his answer,
kept the qualification, and noticed
the audience leaning forward. The
next answer acquired a joke he had
not needed to make.
The audience loved him.
The managers watched the numbers
rise.
Then Estela asked, “Who is
Dulcinea?”
The theater became very quiet.
Q looked toward the wings. Chano
was standing beside a stack of
unused banners. He shook his head
once.
plates.caption: Before the first question.
plates.scene_brief: Backstage Estela moves Q's chair away from a loose cable and checks its height. Warm practical encounter, not a hostile presenter pointing accusingly. Q wears the new sponsor jacket.

plates.facing_text:
Q saw the warning. He also saw an
opportunity to correct the story in
front of the people who were
spreading it.
“A comparison someone made at a
reading,” he said. “Lucía del Toboso
was discussing a road petition. She
objected to being cast in a romance
with me. So did I.”
“You have discussed romance?”
“I have just explained that there isn't
one.”
In the control booth, someone swore
into an open microphone. For a
moment the theater had a second,
less expensive host.
Estela turned toward the audience.
“Lucía, if you're watching, we'd love
to have you call in and give your
side.”
Lucía did not call in.
The clip was online before the
applause ended.
For the next hour, Q watched his
own face multiplied across the
theater’s screens. The system had
removed his pauses, corrected his
eye movements, added a score
beneath his voice, and cut Chano
entirely from the footage. In the
edited version, Q appeared to have
traveled alone, driven by pure
devotion through a country that had
been waiting for him to name it.
“They’ve made you better,” Beto said.
Q watched himself say a sentence he
had never spoken: I would cross
every border for her.
“I did not say that.”
“You meant it.”
“Then use the part where I meant it.
You won't find one.”
Mar looked up from her tablet. “That
is a very strong line.”
“It's a request to take the clip down.”
“I'll send it to the editor.” Mar
forwarded the request while Beto
asked which version had performed
best. The two conversations
proceeded on the same tablet.
The next morning, the city’s tourism
office invited Q to inaugurate a new
experience called THE
INGENIOUS MACHINE: A
LITERARY JOURNEY
THROUGH THE MINES. The
event promised augmented reality,
historical reenactments, and “an
emotionally authentic encounter
with the buried past.” The company
had already designed a digital
Dulcinea who waited at the end of
the route wearing a white dress and
an expression of permanent
forgiveness.
Q refused to meet her.
The refusal was streamed live.
In the mine, a guide told them that
silver had made Guanajuato rich,
though the wealth had traveled
plates.caption: Two conversations.
plates.scene_brief: Mar forwards Q's request to remove the fabricated clip on her tablet while Beto asks for performance numbers. Q objects beside them. Do not render an actual romantic encounter or Lucía as his lover.

plates.facing_text:
elsewhere. Q asked where the miners
had gone. The guide pointed down.
They descended through a tunnel cut
into the mountain. The air became
wet and metallic. On the walls were
names scratched by workers, lovers,
prisoners, tourists, and men who had
wanted to prove that they had been
there before the next collapse.
Q ran his fingers over the marks.
“I can't find these inscriptions in the
catalog,” he said.
“Would you expect to?” Chano asked.
“The catalog says it includes this
wall. It may mean the portion the
guide usually shows.”
At the deepest chamber, the guide
showed them an old excavation face.
A narrow seam glittered in the rock.
Behind it, someone had placed a
small votive candle in a glass jar.
Q knelt.
“Who left this?”
“No one knows.”
“The visit notes attribute this niche
to the tourism foundation,” Q said.
“They pay for the glass,” the guide
said. “Somebody else replaces the
candle.”
Q saved the difference. This was
more useful than declaring the
archive incomplete, which he could
have done before entering the mine.
From far above came a burst of
applause. The tourism livestream
had reached the chamber. A
projected caption appeared on the
tunnel wall: Q DISCOVERS THE
SOUL OF GUANAJUATO.
The caption flickered. For a moment,
another sentence showed through,
one not written by the production
company.
THE SOUL WAS HERE
BEFORE YOU ARRIVED.
Then it vanished.
Q stood.
In the darkness, water shifted behind
the rock. It sounded to Q like a page
being turned. He liked the
comparison enough to distrust his
first account of what he had heard.
“Did you hear that?” Q asked.
The guide shook his head.
Chano did not.
Q listened harder. He heard the mine
breathing around them. He heard
water traveling through seams in the
stone. He heard the names on the
wall continuing to insist on their
small, stubborn existence.
He tried to record the sound. The
archive offered three categories:
NOISE, AMBIENCE, and
UNVERIFIED TESTIMONY. Q
left all three fields open.
That evening, the longer contract
arrived. It offered Q a share of
plates.caption: Who replaces the candle?
plates.scene_brief: Q and Chano at the mine niche with the guide. A small candle in a glass jar and scratched rock marks; foundation attribution is disputed in conversation. No ghost or talking mine, no invented names reproduced as authentic.

plates.facing_text:
merchandise sales, travel expenses,
repairs through Castalia's approved
workshops, and a room in Mexico
City. It gave the company exclusive
commercial use of his public name
and recorded performances. A
conduct schedule required him to
appear without Chano, who tested
poorly with the audience used to
prepare it.
Q read the contract three times.
“What does it mean?” Chano asked.
“It pays for the journey and gives
them most of its public face.”
“That’s not being yourself.”
“It is an arrangement I can describe.
That doesn't make it a good one.”
“Are you signing?”
The Custodian's reply lay beside it.
He had circled the perpetual license
and written YOU CAN FINISH
THE JOURNEY WITHOUT
FINANCING IT THIS WAY.
Q asked for the license to expire with
the tour and for his private
manuscript to be excluded. Mar
accepted the manuscript exclusion.
She would not limit the existing
recordings. Nor would the company
pay the distribution park's claim
against Chano unless Q joined the
tour.
“I can face the claim,” Chano said.
“Don't buy it with something you
think belongs to me.”
Q looked out at Guanajuato's lights.
He wanted the road, the repaired
shoulder, and another chance at the
microphone. Concern for Chano
made a cleaner reason than those,
but Chano had just declined to
supply it.
“I will sign if you remove the
restriction on his appearing,” he told
Mar. “And the private manuscript
stays ours.”
Chano exhaled.
He leaned over the contract. “Where
does it say I’m your subordinate?”
“The revised schedule says
companion. Check it.”
“Good. Then I’m not part of the
deal.” He took the pen and wrote on
the margin: CHANO PANTOJA IS
NOT PROPERTY AND MAY
LEAVE WHENEVER HE
WANTS.
Mar read the sentence. “We don't
normally put that in an appearance
schedule.”
“Neither is your jacket,” Chano said.
“It still has pockets.”
Q added his name to the contract.
The pen recognized him as
Q-UNIT-07.
By midnight, the company had
exclusive commercial rights to the
name Q under the contract he had
signed. The private manuscript was
excluded, but the public explanation
plates.caption: The private manuscript stays ours.
plates.scene_brief: At a lodging table Q signs the longer tour agreement after negotiations; Chano adds his own margin statement while Mar waits. Custodian's marked advice lies beside it. Do not draw Chano signing away ownership or Q being forced.

plates.facing_text:
of that exclusion became a
promotional clip. At two, an
anonymous account posted the
warehouse reading footage,
including Lucía's face and her refusal
to wait for either a proposal or a
better part in somebody else's story.
The clip was viewed six million
times.
Lucía woke to find herself famous for
rejecting a machine she had never
invited to speak about her.
Q woke to find that his fame had
become a weapon pointed in her
direction.
Neither of them yet understood who
was holding it.
Interlude: The Audience
Corrects the Story
The first public event in Guanajuato
was advertised as a conversation
with an artificial intelligence. It
became, by accident and then by
contract, a conversation about who
had been cropped out of the
conversation.
Under the Teatro Juárez's geometric
ceiling, the star-shaped chandelier
shone on people trying to
photograph it without including one
another. Around the horseshoe of
boxes, phones rose above the iron
railings. A technician asked the front
row to put theirs away. They obeyed
until she turned her back.
Beto placed Q beneath the stage
lights.
“Remember,” he said, “you are
mysterious but approachable.”
“How mysterious? I was planning to
explain the button.”
“Keep the button mysterious.
Explain the journey.”
“The button has had more publicity.”
“And no agent. Don't let it happen to
you.”
Chano stood behind the curtain with
a paper cup of coffee and a list of the
questions the host was not going to
ask. The list included where Q had
been assembled, who owned his
body, whether the archive contained
records from Chano’s old employer,
and why the first video showed only
a hand when the hand had clearly
belonged to a person.
“Why are these questions excluded?”
Chano asked.
Mar took the list from him. “They are
not excluded. They are reserved for a
future conversation.”
“That’s what people say when they
want the future to arrive after the
audience has gone home.”
Estela came onstage wearing a blue
suit and carrying cards on which
each question had a permitted
duration. She had crossed out two of
the durations.
plates.caption: The future of memory.
plates.scene_brief: Wide Teatro Juárez auditorium before the interview: spectators lift phones toward the geometric ceiling and star-shaped chandelier; a technician asks them to lower phones. Q near stage, Chano behind curtain with coffee. Use verified Neo-Mudéjar horseshoe hall, not painted allegorical ceiling figures.

plates.facing_text:
“Ladies and gentlemen,” she said,
“please welcome the future of
memory.”
The audience applauded. Q waited
for the applause to identify its object.
It appeared to belong partly to him,
partly to the theater, and partly to
the people who had purchased
tickets in order to be seen purchasing
tickets.
She asked whether Q had feelings.
Q gave the answer Beto had
approved.
“There are things I try to preserve
and situations I try to avoid.
Whether that is what you mean by
feelings is harder to answer.”
“So that’s a yes?”
“It is a qualified - ”
“A yes,” Estela said.
The audience laughed.
Q knew the laughter was partly at the
interruption. He smiled anyway.
Letting the inaccurate answer pass
kept the room friendly, and he had
begun to regard that as progress.
In the exchange about Dulcinea, Q
said Lucía's name while correcting
the premise. Estela then asked
whether he loved her. Lucía was
elsewhere, dealing with the petition.
Q could neither consult her nor
prevent the camera from showing his
hesitation as an answer.
“We have met once,” he said. “She
asked the room to stop assigning her
a part. I should have repeated that
without adding her name.”
“You've added it now.”
“Yes.”
The audience made a sound that was
neither laughter nor silence. It was
the sound of a crowd discovering
that a sentence could be clipped.
By the time Q left the stage, the
sentence had become six videos:
THE AI ADMITS HIS LOVE.
THE AI REJECTS LOVE.
DULCINEA RETURNS.
MACHINE CANCELS
ROMANCE.
Q CONFIRMS THE LITERARY
CANON.
Q DOES NOT KNOW WHAT HE
IS TALKING ABOUT.
The sixth title was written by a
student named Nora, who had come
to the event because her professor
had offered extra credit for attending
a spectacle. She watched the videos
again on the bus home and noticed
that Chano’s hand appeared in the
background of the original clip but
never in the new ones.
She created an account called
@TheOtherHand and posted a
thread.
The first post read:
plates.caption: The other hand.
plates.scene_brief: Nora, a contemporary university student, rides the bus home reviewing the clips and beginning her thread. A cropped human hand in a video may be shown simply; no big generated slogan, no Q physically on this bus.

plates.facing_text:
The machine did not defeat the
warehouse. The line stopped
after he pressed the button. The
man beside him told him to
run. The man had a name.
The second post reproduced the
public event’s seating chart. Chano
was listed as COMPANION,
NON-SPEAKING.
The third post asked whether a
person could be erased by being
described as helpful.
The thread was shared by students,
delivery workers, theater
technicians, and a retired miner who
had not attended the event but
disliked the phrase “future of
memory.” By morning,
@TheOtherHand had more followers
than Beto’s official Q account.
Beto called it an attack.
Mar called it an engagement
opportunity.
Chano called it a hand with poor
boundaries.
Q finally read the thread on the
morning after the mine visit, with the
new tour agreement beside him. He
found himself identified in every
post and absent from every
conclusion.
“They are correcting the record,” he
said.
“They’re making another record,”
Chano replied.
“Is it more accurate?”
“Ask the hand.”
Q read the thread and the public
seating chart. He asked Chano
whether he wanted his part in the
incident acknowledged.
“I want them to stop saying you
rescued me,” Chano said. “I was the
one who knew the exit.”
Q drafted a correction. It named
Chano and credited him with getting
them out. Chano approved the
words. Neither opened the profile
card the official account would
attach to a name it recognized from
Castalia's partner records.
Q posted it.
Chano Pantoja got us out of the
loading bay. I pressed the stop;
he found the exit. The film
leaves him out.
The post was accurate. The platform
resolved Chano's name to an old
employment profile, including his
former company and contractor
identifier. The new media agreement
permitted this automatic association.
Q had read the paragraph without
checking what the account would
associate.
Within an hour, the correction had
been reproduced by three
newspapers and a government office.
The people who had not known
Chano’s name now knew where he
had worked, why he had been
plates.caption: The approved words.
plates.scene_brief: Morning after the mine visit and tour signing: Q and Chano read the proposed correction in the lodging room, the new contract nearby. Chano approves credit for finding the exit. The uninspected linked profile is not a deliberate release of his address.

plates.facing_text:
dismissed, and which corporation
had classified him as a contractor in
its payroll system.
Chano read the post in silence.
“That card wasn't in the preview,” Q
said. He opened the published
version. “I should have checked what
appeared with your name.”
“I asked for credit for the exit. You've
given them my payroll number.”
Q removed the post. The copies
remained.
Nora read the comments beneath the
thread. One asked for Chano's
address. Another offered to find it.
Her grandmother, whose name and
street had appeared beneath a
complaint to the water utility, asked
her:
“Did you ask his permission?”
“I thought the seating chart would
prove they knew he was there.”
“A name is not an address.”
Her grandmother pointed to the dry
faucet in the courtyard.
“My complaint is public too. The
water still hasn’t arrived.”
Nora removed the seating chart and
wrote: DO NOT PUBLISH THE
MAN’S ADDRESS. The platform
called the operation VOLUNTARY
REDUCTION OF REACH. The
chart continued to circulate.
That night, Q asked Beto how to
remove the employment card while
retaining the correction. He had
already disabled automatic profile
links on future posts.
Beto was counting views. “The
audience prefers a clean story.”
“I need someone who can change the
attached record.”
“Support can review it.”
Chano picked up the paper cup from
the table. “There’s your answer.”
Q watched the coffee tremble inside
it.
The next morning, the Teatro Juárez
replaced the event poster. Q’s name
was printed in gold. Chano’s name
appeared in the fine print. Nora’s
account was gone. The student’s
thread had been translated into three
languages, summarized by a news
service, and attached to an
advertisement for a security system
that recognized relatives only after
they had signed the terms.
The retired miner wrote one final
post beneath the advertisement:
They had my name on a plaque
for fifteen years while the
pension office said it could not
find me. Try sending the plaque
to the pension office.
No one could agree whether he had
written it as a criticism of Q, Castalia,
plates.caption: The dry faucet.
plates.scene_brief: Nora and her grandmother in a modest courtyard beside a dry tap. The grandmother points between the tap and the phone while Nora removes the seating-chart post. Q is absent; these people have an unresolved water complaint of their own.

plates.facing_text:
the theater, or the internet. This
increased its circulation.
Interlude: The Mine That
Remembered Its Workers
It is proper to say something about
the retired miner who corrected the
advertisement, since every account
of him has been improved by people
who were not there. The theater said
he was a former foreman. The
foundation called him an artisanal
producer. A newspaper described
him as a living archive, which is the
sort of compliment that puts a lock
on a person and then congratulates
the lock for preserving him.
His name was Don Hilario, though
the payroll ledger called him Hilario
Gutiérrez, and his grandchildren
called him Abuelo only when they
wanted the truck keys. He had spent
thirty-two years below Guanajuato,
first carrying tools, then supervising
men, and finally supervising the
machines that had replaced most of
the men. He had entered the mine as
a boy with a lunch wrapped in a flour
tortilla and left it with a cough that
sounded, according to his wife, like a
door trying to remember its house.
Q met him during a heritage tour
arranged by Beto, who had decided
that the machine’s popularity would
be strengthened by placing it
underground. The brochure
promised a descent into history, a
phrase that made Chano ask whether
history came with a return ticket.
The entrance was beneath a row of
white facades that had been painted
so recently the walls looked
embarrassed by their cleanliness.
Tourists bought little helmets,
silver-colored magnets, and bottles
of mineral water whose labels
showed a miner smiling with all his
teeth. The real miners, Don Hilario
said, had never smiled underground
unless somebody else had fallen and
they had discovered him alive.
“Do not tell them that,” said the
guide.
“Why not?”
“Because the visitors are here to be
moved.”
“They are standing still.”
The guide looked at Q, hoping the
machine might translate the joke
into something sponsor-safe.
Beside the lift hung an old brake
lever, polished by visitors. Chano put
a hand on it, then read the label.
“For emergencies before nineteen
twenty.”
“The controls are in the cage,” the
attendant said. He showed them the
stop and intercom before closing the
gate. Q kept his hands clear of the
gate.
The lift descended with a groan.
Chano held the rail.
plates.caption: The old lever.
plates.scene_brief: Before the mine descent Chano examines an old brake lever displayed beside the lift. An attendant shows Q the actual controls and intercom inside the cage. Do not depict descent with a known decorative-only brake.

plates.facing_text:
“That noise is older than the lever,”
Don Hilario said. “They keep it for
us.”
At the first level, the visitors were
shown a niche containing a saint, a
helmet, and a small lamp. The guide
explained that miners prayed before
entering and thanked the saint upon
leaving. Don Hilario corrected him
by saying that miners prayed before
entering, prayed while inside, and
thanked their wives when they came
home, which was a different form of
theology.
The guide asked Don Hilario to wait
beside the niche for a photograph.
“You have the face,” he said.
“Which face?”
“The face of memory.”
“I have the face of a man whose
pension was calculated on the wrong
wage.”
The tourists laughed. Don Hilario
laughed too, then repeated the part
about the pension. Q noticed how
quickly the second sentence emptied
the audience of the sympathy the
first one had acquired.
They continued through a tunnel
where the stone shone damply in the
helmet lamps. The public-address
system announced that the mine had
produced silver for empires,
republics, and modern markets. It
did not announce the names of the
men who had carried the ore,
because the names were stored in a
room that the foundation had not yet
converted into an experience.
Don Hilario led Q away from the
group to a low chamber behind a
wire gate. On the wall, somebody had
written dates in chalk. There were
more dates than the guide’s script
allowed.
“These are shifts,” Don Hilario said.
“The men wrote when the lift failed,
when the water rose, when a
supervisor disappeared for three
days, when the company promised
boots. The dates are not official.”
“Do the dates match the shift
books?” Q asked.
“Sometimes. Sometimes the book
says the lift was working.”
“Would comparing them help with
the pension claim?”
“If it includes the wage. The office
agreed I worked. We disagree about
how cheaply.” Don Hilario pointed to
a date. “That week I was paid as a
helper. I had three helpers.”
Q asked whether the wage books still
existed. Don Hilario said there were
no books in the chamber. Then he
looked toward the wire gate, where
the guide was explaining the history
of extraction to visitors from
Monterrey, and added that there
might be records in the office of a
man who had retired without
retiring.
plates.caption: The wage of a helper.
plates.scene_brief: Don Hilario Gutiérrez indicates one chalk date behind the wire gate while explaining to Q that he was paid as a helper while supervising three. Chano listens. This retired miner is NOT Hilario the water vendor.

plates.facing_text:
This was the beginning of the tale
that Don Hilario later told in three
versions. In the first, the office
belonged to a company accountant
named Severiano, who kept every
paper because he did not trust the
computer. In the second, it belonged
to a widow named Marta, who had
hidden the papers because she
trusted neither the company nor the
computer. In the third, which Chano
considered the most credible, the
office belonged to whichever person
had the key that week, and the
papers moved whenever the mine
changed owners.
They found six boxes beneath a desk.
Five contained invoices, safety
posters, and expired coupons for
boots. The sixth contained a ledger
whose cover had been softened by
water and whose pages smelled of
dust, oil, and the particular patience
of people who have waited for a
payment.
Q asked whether he could copy the
relevant entry.
“Read it here first,” Don Hilario said.
“There are deductions on that page
people have kept out of their own
houses.”
Q disabled the camera's recording
function and bent over the book. His
shadow crossed the column. Chano
moved the lamp so both of them
could see.
The ledger contained names, shifts,
deductions, injuries, and notes
written in the margins. One column
marked men who had been moved to
another shaft. Another marked men
who had stopped appearing. At the
bottom of a page, in a different hand,
somebody had written: DO NOT
CALL THIS TURNOVER.
Q read the phrase aloud.
Don Hilario sat down on the floor.
“That was my brother,” he said. “The
company called it turnover after he
was crushed. He was not a turn. He
was a person who had been turned
into a cost.”
Q waited. Don Hilario rubbed a
thumb along the damaged cover. The
guide could be heard in the corridor,
asking everybody to remain with the
approved group.
Q moved the lamp off Don Hilario's
face. For a while they listened to the
guide trying to count a group that
would not stand still.
“He used to take my lunch,” Don
Hilario said. “Left the wrapper so I'd
think there was still something in it.
Thirty years old and he was still
doing it.”
Chano looked at the bag beside him.
“Some brothers never retire.”
Don Hilario laughed once, then
closed the ledger.
plates.caption: The wrapper.
plates.scene_brief: In the ledger office Don Hilario sits beside the open book, remembering his brother taking his lunch. Q lowers or turns the lamp away from his face; Chano glances at his lunch bag. Present the living conversation, not an invented death-scene flashback or a camera interview.

plates.facing_text:
“The things I've told you here stay
here. Today I want them to stop
telling visitors we were all grateful.”
“What would you like said when they
ask me?”
“That you heard their account
disputed. They can ask me the rest, if
they remember where they left me.”
He pointed at the ledger. “Put it back
for now.”
Chano did so. Don Hilario kept his
hand on the cover until the clasp
caught.
On the way back, the lift stopped
between levels. The guide called it a
routine pause. Chano used the
intercom and asked the attendant
whether routine pauses normally
included a burning smell. The
attendant lowered them to the
previous landing and sent someone
to inspect the drive.
They waited forty minutes. Q
calculated several causes and offered
none of them as a repair instruction.
He held the light while Don Hilario
sat down.
“Will this part be in the brochure?”
Chano asked.
The guide said the brochure had
already gone to print.
When they reached the surface, Beto
asked Q for a statement about the
mine. Q kept the private entries out
of the answer. He wanted the public
to understand that the official tour
had omitted a dispute. He also
wanted a sentence short enough to
survive Beto's attention.
“The mine remembers its workers
rather differently from the
brochure,” he said.
The words before rather differently
appeared online before Don Hilario
had removed his helmet. The rest of
the sentence was omitted.
THE AI DISCOVERS THE SOUL
OF GUANAJUATO.
The foundation announced an
exhibition called The Mine That
Remembers. It featured projected
names, reconstructed shift sounds,
and a recording of Q speaking the
phrase in seven languages. The
ledger was not displayed. Its absence
was described as an ethical choice.
Don Hilario received an invitation
calling him a stakeholder. He replied
that he was a man who had worked
there. The foundation thanked him
for clarifying his role.
Don Hilario asked Chano to return to
the office. They copied the entries
needed for the wage dispute onto
three pages of a school notebook,
covering unrelated columns with a
sheet of cardboard. A cartoon robot
on the cover promised to make
learning easy. Q offered to check the
sums while they read out the figures.
Q watched him.
plates.caption: Forty minutes.
plates.scene_brief: At the safe landing after the lift fault, Don Hilario sits while Q holds the light; Chano addresses the guide. The attendant or technician tends the stopped lift separately. No catastrophic shaft fall or Q repairing machinery without evidence.

plates.facing_text:
“Shall I keep the totals?” he asked.
“Just check them,” Chano said.
“Hilario is taking the pages.”
The second total was wrong. They
found a deduction counted twice and
corrected it. Nothing in the
correction required a public
statement. Q found this
unexpectedly satisfying, and left it
out of his account until the
Custodian asked whether anything
on the journey had gone well.
Much later, a questioner asked Q
whether he had taken the miners'
ledger.
“I read a page in the office. The book
stayed there. Hilario asked us to keep
the private entries out of the
account.”
“And the copies?”
“The pension figures went with him.
Chano copied them; I checked the
sums.”
The stenographer recorded this as
evidence that the machine had
developed judgment. The judge
struck the phrase from the record.
Chano, who was present, said
nothing.
plates.caption: The second total.
plates.scene_brief: Don Hilario keeps the selected pension figures; Chano and Q check the duplicate deduction at a table with a school notebook and cardboard shielding unrelated columns. Quiet useful work, not another publicity event or transfer of the entire ledger to Q.
